blocks.text: Discovery tells a model what tools exist. Invocation is the moment that knowledge turns into action, the model picks a tool, fills in arguments, and something real happens on the other end of the connection.
This is the single most consequential step in the whole MCP request lifecycle, since everything before it is just preparation and everything after it is just interpretation.
This lesson walks through tools/call in full: how arguments get built, how the request travels, and what comes back.
1. From Decision to Call

blocks.alt: A model decides to act and turns that decision into a tool call

blocks.text: A model does not call a tool directly the way a program calls a function. Instead, the model produces a structured statement of intent, essentially saying I want to call this named tool with these arguments, and it is the client that turns that intent into an actual tools/call request sent over the wire. The model never touches the network, never opens a socket, never sees a response until the client has finished the round trip and handed the result back.

This separation matters because it keeps the model's job purely one of reasoning and the client's job purely one of execution. The model decides what should happen, the client and server decide how it actually happens, and neither side needs to know the internal details of the other.

It is a bit like ordering food at a restaurant. You decide what you want and say it out loud, the kitchen actually cooks it, and you never once touch a stove yourself. The model is the person ordering, the server is the kitchen, and the client is the waiter carrying the ticket back and forth.
2. The tools/call Method

blocks.alt: A tools call request returns a result response

blocks.text: The concrete JSON-RPC method is tools/call. It carries two required pieces of information in its params, the name of the tool being invoked and an arguments object holding the values for that tool's inputSchema. The name has to exactly match one of the tools the server returned from tools/list, and the arguments object has to validate against that tool's schema.

Notice how closely this mirrors the inputSchema shown during discovery. The arguments object is not free form, it is the model's best attempt at producing a JSON object that satisfies exactly the schema the server advertised earlier. Anything else the model attaches outside of what the schema describes is either ignored or rejected, depending on the server's own validation strictness.
2.1 Strict vs Lenient Servers

Some servers set additionalProperties to false in their schema and reject any arguments object carrying a field it did not declare, treating an unexpected field as a validation error. Others are more forgiving and simply ignore anything extra. Neither choice is universally correct, a strict server catches a model's mistakes earlier and more clearly, while a lenient server tolerates small drift in how a model phrases a call without breaking outright.

blocks.text: 3. How the Model Builds Arguments

Behind the scenes, the model provider's own machinery is responsible for turning natural language reasoning into a syntactically valid arguments object. When a model decides city should be Paris and units should be celsius, it emits that as structured output, typically JSON, that the client can parse directly without needing to guess at intent from free text.

This is exactly why a well written inputSchema matters so much. The clearer the schema, the fewer malformed or half guessed argument objects a model tends to produce, and the fewer round trips get wasted on a server rejecting an invalid call.
4. Validating Arguments Before Executing

blocks.alt: Arguments that pass validation get executed while invalid ones are rejected

blocks.text: A well behaved server never trusts an incoming arguments object blindly, even though the model tried its best to match the schema. Models occasionally produce a string where a number was expected, omit a required field, or include an extra property that was never declared. The server's first job on receiving a tools/call request is to validate the arguments against its own schema before running any real logic.

blocks.title: Validate at the boundary
blocks.content: Schema validation belongs at the very edge of the server, before any business logic runs. Letting an invalid argument object reach deeper code paths is how obscure crashes and confusing bugs end up surfacing far away from their real cause.

blocks.text: 4.1 A Rejected Call

Seeing an actual rejection makes the value of boundary validation concrete. If a model sends a units value the schema never listed as a valid enum option, the server should catch this immediately and return a clear tool level error rather than attempting to run the underlying weather lookup with a nonsense unit.
5. Executing the Tool

Once arguments pass validation, the server actually runs whatever logic the tool represents, calling an internal function, hitting a database, making an outbound API request, or triggering a physical device. This is the step where the real world changes, sending the email, moving the robot arm, charging the card. Everything before this point was just plumbing to get valid arguments to this exact moment.

How long this step takes and how it is implemented is entirely up to the server, MCP has no opinion on it. A tool can be a single line of code or an orchestration of five downstream services, the protocol only cares about the request going in and the result coming out.

blocks.title: The protocol stops at the boundary
blocks.content: MCP defines the shape of the request and the result, never the implementation in between. Two servers exposing an identical get_weather tool could be backed by wildly different systems internally, and a client would have no way to tell, nor any reason to care.

blocks.text: 6. The Result Comes Back

After execution finishes, the server sends back a tools/call response carrying a result object. That result contains a content array, typically holding one or more pieces of text, and an isError flag indicating whether the call succeeded or failed. The next lesson goes deep on exactly what shapes this content can take, for this lesson it is enough to see the basic envelope.
7. One Call, One Response

blocks.alt: One tool call maps to exactly one response

blocks.text: Every tools/call request corresponds to exactly one response, matched by the id field carried on both messages. There is no concept in the base protocol of a single call producing multiple separate result messages, a call is a strict request and reply pair. Tools that take a long time to finish still ultimately produce one final result, they just may emit progress notifications along the way, which the async tools lesson later in this module covers in detail.

blocks.text: 8. Multiple Tool Calls in One Turn

blocks.alt: One turn can include several tool calls at once

blocks.text: A model is often allowed to request several tool calls within a single turn, for example looking up weather in three different cities before writing a single combined summary. Each of those is still its own independent tools/call request and response pair, matched by its own id, even though they might be issued back to back or in parallel by the client.

code.content:
# A model might request three calls in one turn
calls = [
  {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}},
  {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Tokyo"}},
  {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Nairobi"}},
]
results = [client.call("tools/call", {"name": c["name"], "arguments": c["arguments"]}) for c in calls]

blocks.text: The client is free to execute independent calls concurrently to save time, as long as it keeps every result correctly associated with the call that produced it before handing all of them back to the model together.
9. Where in the Turn This Happens
A model's turn does not end the moment it decides to call a tool.

The typical flow is that the model emits a tool call, the client executes it and appends the result to the conversation, and then the model is invoked again with that new information now visible, continuing the same logical turn until it eventually produces a plain text answer with no further tool calls pending.
From a user's perspective this whole exchange usually looks like one seamless response, even though several tools/call round trips may have happened underneath it.
9.1 Guarding Against Runaway Loops

Because the model itself decides when to stop calling tools, a bug in reasoning or a confusing tool result can in principle send it into a long, repetitive chain of calls that never converges on a plain text answer. Responsible clients cap the number of tool call rounds allowed within a single turn, and surface a clear stop with an explanation once that cap is hit, rather than letting the loop run indefinitely and burn time and money.

blocks.title: A cap is a safety net, not a design goal
blocks.content: Hitting the cap regularly on a particular tool is usually a signal that the tool's description or result format is confusing the model, not that the cap itself needs to be raised.

blocks.text: 10. Timeouts and Slow Tools

Because a client is waiting on a response before it can continue the conversation, every tools/call implicitly has a timeout, whether that is written down explicitly or just enforced by whatever transport or client library is in use. A tool that quietly takes ninety seconds to answer a request meant to complete in five will often trigger a timeout error on the client side well before the server ever finishes, leaving both sides in an inconsistent state.

blocks.title: Slow tools need a different pattern
blocks.content: A tool that genuinely takes a long time should not just be a slow version of a normal call. It should use the async patterns, progress notifications and polling, covered in the async tools lesson later in this module, rather than forcing the client to sit on an open connection and hope.

blocks.text: 11. Errors at the Transport Layer vs the Tool Layer

blocks.alt: A transport layer error is compared against a tool layer error

blocks.text: It helps to separate two very different kinds of failure that can happen around a tools/call. A transport level failure means the request never even reached a working server, a dropped connection, a malformed JSON-RPC envelope, a completely unknown method name. A tool level failure means the request arrived fine, the server understood exactly what was being asked, but the tool itself could not complete successfully, for example a city name that does not exist.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Failure Type","Example","How It Surfaces"],"rows":[["Transport level","Connection drops mid request","JSON-RPC error object, or no response at all"],["Tool level","City not found in weather service","A normal tools/call response with isError set to true"]]}

blocks.text: The distinction matters a great deal for how a model should react. A transport failure usually means retrying the exact same call might work once the connection recovers. A tool level failure usually means the arguments or the underlying request itself need to change before trying again, retrying identically will just fail the same way a second time.
12. Idempotency and Repeated Calls

blocks.alt: A repeated call to an idempotent tool produces the same result

blocks.text: Some tools are safe to call more than once with the same arguments and get the same effect, reading a file, checking a status. Others are absolutely not, sending a payment, creating a duplicate order. A model deciding whether to retry a call that seemingly failed needs to know which kind of tool it is dealing with, and that information should live directly in the tool's own description written during discovery, not be something the model has to guess at invocation time.

items: Idempotent tools, safe to call again if a response seems to have been lost, for example get_account_balance
Non idempotent tools, unsafe to blindly retry, for example charge_card or send_message
A description that explicitly states which category a tool falls into removes an entire class of retry related mistakes

blocks.text: 13. Arguments That Reference Prior Results

It is common for a later tool call in the same turn to use a value produced by an earlier one, for example calling search_customer to get an id, then calling get_orders with that same id as an argument. MCP itself has no special mechanism for this, it is purely the model's own reasoning that carries a value forward from one result into the next call's arguments, exactly like a person copying a number from one screen into another form.

code.content:
# First call
search_result = call_tool("search_customer", {"name": "Alex Kim"})
# search_result content includes {"customer_id": "cus_8841"}

# Second call reuses that value directly in its arguments
call_tool("get_orders", {"customer_id": "cus_8841"})

blocks.text: 14. What the Client Logs and Shows the User
Most MCP hosts surface some visible trace of an invocation to the user, at minimum the tool name and a short summary of the arguments, sometimes the full request and response.

This is not part of the protocol itself, but it is one of the most important trust building features a client can offer, since it lets a person catch a model about to do something unexpected before the effect actually happens, particularly for tools the user has flagged as needing confirmation, which the permissions lesson covers in depth.

Good invocation logging shows the tool name, the exact arguments sent, and the exact result received, in a form a non technical user can still parse at a glance. Burying this behind a raw JSON dump defeats the purpose, since almost no user will actually read it before approving or dismissing it.

A short line like called get_weather for Paris, got back 18 degrees and partly cloudy tells a user everything they need in one glance, and is worth far more than a collapsed JSON blob nobody ever expands.
15. A Complete Round Trip

Putting every piece together, a single tool invocation looks like this from start to finish, a request built from a schema, sent over the wire, executed on a server, and a result handed back that the model then reads as part of the very next thing it says.
Worked Example

Consider a travel assistant with a book_flight tool whose inputSchema requires origin, destination, and date. A user asks to book a flight from Chicago to Denver next Friday. The model resolves next Friday to an actual calendar date, builds an arguments object with all three required fields filled in, and the client sends a single tools/call request.

The server validates the arguments, confirms a matching flight exists, actually reserves the seat, and returns a result containing a confirmation number. The model reads that confirmation number back from the content array and reports it to the user in plain language, the user never sees the raw JSON at all, only the client's rendering of it and the model's summary.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating a tool level error, isError true, the same as a transport failure and blindly retrying a non idempotent call
Sending arguments that do not match the schema returned by discovery, for example a string where the schema requires a number
Assuming a client will show a user every argument sent, when many hosts only surface a short summary unless configured otherwise
Forgetting that a slow tool called synchronously through tools/call risks a client side timeout rather than a graceful async flow
Building multi step call chains that copy values between calls without checking the earlier result actually contains the field being referenced
Not distinguishing idempotent from non idempotent tools in a description, leaving a model to guess whether retrying is safe

blocks.text: Practice

Given a tool named create_calendar_event with an inputSchema requiring title, start_time, and end_time, write the exact tools/call request a client would send to schedule a meeting called Design Review from 2pm to 3pm on July 10th 2026. Then write a plausible successful result for that call.
Then write one sentence describing whether create_calendar_event is idempotent, and what should happen if a model tries to call it twice with identical arguments by mistake.
Key Takeaway

Invocation is the tools/call request and response pair that turns a model's decision into a real action, carrying a tool name and a validated arguments object out, and a content bearing result back. It is a strict one request, one response cycle, and everything the model learns from a call, success or failure, arrives entirely through that single result.

The next lesson zooms into the arguments side of that exchange in real depth, exploring how a well designed inputSchema handles required and optional fields, defaults, nested objects, arrays, and enums, and what separates a schema that is easy for a model to fill in correctly from one that invites mistakes.
